title: Let the Raptures Commence
description: 8 × 45min British black comedy. Four billion people sorted by a child's layout decision. Eight episode outlines; Episode One revised to 42min with washing up (26 shots FIX 4 pendant mother always had it), Danny and Jodie (21) and cops second beat (6); ep3 cold open angels 15 shots, ep4 Pat cold open dusk 16 shots continuous into Scene 2 old lady 35 shots replaced by ep5 Night at Pat's 51 shots no CCTV two grammars only (cops static 32mm windscreen handheld only for violence, Danny/Jodie handheld close dark red torchlight, demons only in torch beam), Number Fourteen 13 shots, therapy class 26 shots brown rationed. Fixes: prologue 12 pockets tracker + flash 24f fastening, shot31 cut ERROR→UNDO?, Ep1 Sc3 shot18 cut +23-24 own room drawer practical, Martin auction pre-rapture flashback, Ep3 meeting trimmed recruitment only.

acts.title: Episode 1 — No mechanism revealed
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

The mugging. Nina Sc 1 — St Jude's and the rapture. The cops — birds, arrest ourselves, the taser. Nina Sc 3 — washing up and aftermath, the pendant (her mother's, always had it, not Deborah's bedside), the first vision, she drives. Martin's auction — marked as pre-rapture flashback, since the machine must have been in Max's room for eight weeks. Then Danny and Jodie — first appearance, three weeks in, they do this now and she's better at it (handheld, tight, dark, red practical light, never a clean wide). Then the cops second beat — static two-shot from the bonnet, same bottle untouched, ends comic thread worse than it started (ninety seconds). Tag: 1980, ending on NO. Roughly 42 minutes before tag.

acts.title: Episode 2 — There's an afterlife and it's badly run
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

Limbo: the family, the branches of Christianity, the seventy-two virgins, the husband led away. Danny and Jodie's first raid. Hell's intake floor. Nina's first wrong lockup; she acquires Alan.

acts.title: Episode 3 — Blanks, and both sides come down
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

Demons and angels arrive, badly. The blanks established. The cops invent a worthless test. Danny and Jodie recruited by the underground group. Brown water. Martin comes home to a collection and no son.

acts.title: Episode 4 — The old lady
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

Jodie on the settee, Danny in the kitchen, the knife and fork, the fork through the forearm, the bottles by the gate. Scout hut recruitment trimmed to recruitment only — twelve litres, rota, 'tins don't count', Jodie working out who's stealing. Grandma/dog and nun moved to Episode Five therapy class.

acts.title: Episode 5 — Therapy + the night at Pat's
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

Therapy class revised — 26 shots, INT. THE SCOUT HUT DAY, handheld close faces circle not quite circle red fire door light tarpaulin never wide. Hi-vis clipboard facilitator, Sue 50s blameless furious, Carl 30s knows what he did, Derek 60s sober 22 years insufferable, Pauline 40s wants to write to someone, Danny/Jodie at edge not participating. Safe space/scout hut, laminated sheet writing down who doesn't, never done anything/cat note, forty years careful Linda horrible, everybody's problem, clerical mistake/Because, who do you write to/look into it, Carl quiet too quickly nothing they'd take you for, modesty/Jodie does not, Rosemary next door dog rug Thursday went up straight up, that bad, long hold silence dead dog demolishes room (protection), what we're for invented on spot (protection), kept us back work/keep order doctrine, promoted maintain order, divine mandate in ninety seconds no objections, Derek moment of clarity 2003, end of world not same as divorce very similar, one day at a time most useful thing in eight weeks, not pleased, empty chair Brian went out Tuesday, nobody follows up, Jodie at edge adults guessing, Danny sleeve over bandage, final wide brown and rationed water not two days left. Protections: Carl never says what he did. Doctrine needs time to harden before 7-8. Then the night at Pat's — 51 shots, EXT./INT. PAT'S ROAD AND HOUSE NIGHT, replaces previous Pat's house version. No CCTV anywhere. Two grammars only: cops static two-shot through windscreen 32mm locked off handheld only for violence, Danny and Jodie handheld close dark red torchlight, demons only ever seen in someone's torch beam. Kath Ray Danny Jodie Pat Malcolm Neil (50s blank talks about flooring). Stakeout crisps bottle untouched, six bottles at gate, Jodie door under stairs nobody doesn't look, rules taking him off himself, Pat facing fireplace, DO NOT FEED, Neil chained bike lock 1234 old people laminate membrane, slippers tea mouth too wide tea still held, chaotic tea everywhere Neil walks past, head turned all way round, first handheld for cops Police Stop there please, taser form, cuffs their faces go, secure premises, side by side Pat Malcolm knife fork fish slice black eyes smiling Out, sprint everyone in seatbelt, doesn't start it starts, Bring my bottles back love same framing as shot 2, five people in car grammar restored That was drugs condition, arrested forever till something opens, Say sorry I can only apologise first one delighted, evidence cup holder, I'd have to check, laminate, tiny headlights 135mm CUT. Max misspelling flashback remains.

acts.title: Episode 6 — Dry
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

The taps fail completely, upstairs dead system-wide, doctrine from therapy class hardening into religion. Group starts acting on 'maintain order' in 7-8. One day at a time remains only useful advice. Nina gets a bearing that isn't wrong and is found by people who've decided she's a saint (nun rumour from therapy points at her). The cops arrest a demon and paperwork won't stick. Max flashback: stat bars.

acts.title: Episode 7 — Convergence
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

Four parties, four wrong reasons, one postcode. Martin already there with the machine plugged in, trying to make it play something. Limbo: someone in administration realises nobody is auditing them either. Max flashback: "just clear our past attempts."

acts.title: Episode 8 — The arcade
acts.description:
45-minute episode outline, not a completed shooting script.

Everyone in one building, all wrong about why. Martin defends his collection from people trying to save the world. The cops arrest people in sequence. Demons and angels arrive simultaneously and each assumes the other is what they came for. Upstairs: Jodie gets through because she's eleven and ignored; Nina can't read the menu; Max knows where the fields are. The reversal won't authorise — Limbo administration is protecting the outage, because a stalled queue means nobody audits them. Nina wins an argument at a desk. Then the correction: not a rewind, but a bid on an auction lot, placed by a nun, outbidding Martin for the box the machine is in. ENTER. No flash, no sound.

scenes.lightingNotes: Handheld, tight, dark, red practical light. Never a clean wide. Dry, deadpan British black comedy, never grief or a horror performance.

scenes.lightingNotes: Static two-shot from the bonnet, plus a wide from across the road. The same bottle of water in the cup holder, untouched. Dry, deadpan British black comedy, never a punchline.

scenes.title: Cold open — the recovery angels
scenes.location: EXT./INT. A PARK AND A GARDEN CENTRE
scenes.description: Hariel and Soqed locate nothing in an advert. The unnamed blank between the pallets is nobody's and joins no cast list.
scenes.lightingNotes: The opposite of Hell's surveillance: immaculate. Locked off, perfectly composed, centred, slightly too symmetrical. Wide lenses, everything in focus, beautiful light. It looks like an advert, and that is the joke: the angels have made themselves look tremendous and they are of no use whatsoever. No score, no stings; nothing is remarked upon.

scenes.title: The first wrong lockup
scenes.location: EXT./INT. ROADS AND AN INDUSTRIAL ESTATE
scenes.description: Nina drives out on a pendant bearing, opens two wrong lockups, and acquires Alan. Locked off, wide, deep focus, daylight, symmetrical. The camera never follows Nina. Long lenses for the road. Only the vision is handheld. Dry and procedural; Nina is unimpressed throughout, never amazed or afraid. The vision is the tracker's recorded view, not divine revelation.
scenes.lightingNotes: Daylight throughout, deep focus, symmetrical locked-off framings. Long lenses for the road. Only the vision breaks the grammar: handheld, broken, wrong aspect ratio, dropped frames, blown out, a hiss.

scenes.title: Both sides come down — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Demons and angels arrive, badly. Keep faction coverage separate; no invented shared scene. Demons retain fixed surveillance grammar on earth. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: A worthless screening method — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Blanks established. The cops invent a test around I can only apologise and never doubt it. Half of real humanity says it too. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: The interview
scenes.description: Episode three circles what a blank is from three angles and gets it wrong three times: the angels' cold open, the cops' worthless test, and Hell's five-hour interview that leaves with Wales. The comedy is in the timecode and the stillness; nothing reacts except Tamsin's pen.
scenes.lightingNotes: Fixed high-corner surveillance cameras, 4:3, slight fisheye, faint burnt-in timecode. Cut between fixed angles only. The camera never moves and never gets close. The timecode runs on across the cuts so the audience can see how long this has been going. Dry, deadpan British black comedy; no score, no stings, no reaction inserts.

scenes.title: Recruited / brown water — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Danny and Jodie recruited by the underground group. Brown water. Tight red practical handheld coverage; no full-room tableau. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: A collection and no son — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Martin comes home to a collection and no son. Aggrieved, not grieving. Flat, fluorescent, off-centre. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: Cold open — Pat's house
scenes.description: A demon keeping house at dusk while Graham is chained under the floor: the photographs, the sweet tin, the cupboard of water she never drinks, Malcolm washing to the elbow, Graham's apology from behind a locked door, and one smile at an empty window. She is waiting for nothing; the burglars pick her house by chance.
scenes.lightingNotes: Fixed high-corner surveillance cameras, 4:3, slight fisheye, faint burnt-in timecode. Cut between fixed angles only. The camera never moves and never gets close. Dusk at the first timecode, dark by the last. The blank is already under the floor before anyone knocks, and the apology arrives from behind a locked door; she is waiting for nothing and the burglars pick her house by chance. Dry, deadpan British black comedy; no score, no stings.

scenes.title: Pat's house — the old lady
scenes.description: Scene 2, after the cold open: Jodie audited over squash in the lamplit front room while Danny finds the water cupboard by torchlight. The violence is silent and domestic — the exact rhythm of someone eating a meal — and her grammar returns mid-sentence. Malcolm comes up at the end to a cupboard ajar and I've made a friend. This is NOT Number Fourteen.
scenes.lightingNotes: Two grammars in one house, never blended within a shot. Front room: lamplit, warm, flat, frontal, static, tidy — hers. Kitchen and garden: handheld, close, dark, red torchlight — Danny and Jodie's. The cut between rooms is a cut between two different programmes. Shots 31-32 switch to fixed high-corner 4:3 surveillance with burnt-in timecode; shots 33-35 snap back to the Crane grammar, abruptly.

scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Grandma/dog story and nun rumour moved to Episode Five therapy class. Hi-vis announces meeting at half four about 'why us', which Danny doesn't attend. scenes.lightingNotes: Handheld, close, faces. A circle of chairs that isn't quite a circle. Red from the fire door light and a tarpaulin over a window. Never a clean establishing wide. Dry, deadpan British black comedy, never grief or a horror performance. No score, no reaction inserts. Protections: shot 13 silence long — dead dog demolishes room; hi-vis 'what we're for' visibly invented on spot not doctrine; Carl never says what he did, in this scene or any other.

scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Max flashback: the misspelling of The Raptors. He is alive and unreachable, not a present-day participant. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Four parties converge on one postcode for four wrong reasons. People dying of water failure dully. scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Martin is already there with the machine plugged in, trying to make it play something. His fluorescent, flat, off-centre grammar still applies in episode seven. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: Nobody is auditing us — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Someone in administration realises nobody is auditing them either. This official is not silently assigned to Brenda or Gordon. Limbo is unaffected by time. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: Just clear our past attempts — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Max flashback: just clear our past attempts. He means two seasons of bad placements. Minimising the window sends the signal. ERROR→UNDO? cut (prologue shot 31). Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Martin defends his collection, cops arrest people in sequence, demons and angels arrive together and each assumes the other is the target. All grammars collapse to neutral ordinary coverage. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: The menu / the desk / ENTER — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Jodie gets through because she is eleven and ignored. Nina cannot read the menu; Max knows where the fields are, but the bible retains flashbacks only. Limbo protects the outage. Nina wins an argument at a desk. The correction is an auction bid outbidding Martin, not a rewind. ENTER. No flash, sound or score. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

scenes.title: The scout hut
scenes.description: The scene after the violence. He is bleeding, he has to explain nothing to anyone, and the group's only interest is the water. Four holes in a row that everyone decides not to see.
scenes.lightingNotes: Handheld, tight, close, red practical sources only: a camping lantern and the fire door light. Never a clean wide. Dry, deadpan British black comedy, never grief or a horror performance. No score, no reaction inserts; nobody asks where anything came from.

scenes.title: Number Fourteen
scenes.description: A water stop governed by house rules and an unfinished complaint to the council. Handheld, tight, dark. Red practical sources only. Never a wide establishing shot; never show a whole room. Dry, deadpan British black comedy, not noir, horror performance or tragedy. No pathos, no grief, no score, no reaction inserts. The table set for six is not played; the listener is never shown. This is not Pat's house.
scenes.lightingNotes: Red practical sources only: the letterbox, red dashboard indicators and the kettle's red indicator. Deep darkness outside those small pools. No white, blue, teal, sodium or daylight fill; red is a physical source, never an overall colour grade. Jodie's collar headlamp stays off.

scenes.title: SOLD / just one question — outline
scenes.description: OUTLINE ONLY — not a numbered shooting script. Shutter down, machine unopened in the dark. Lot sticker: number, date, SOLD. Then timeless Limbo, the same queue, a man at the desk with one question. No epilogue, no faces, no resolution for anyone. Location/time are provisional unless specified by the bible.

characters.name: Sister Nina Doyle
characters.description: Runs St Jude's, a residential house for people the system gave up on. Self-sufficient, can re-plumb a building, lies fluently to authority; gentle with the genuinely broken, brutal with anyone coasting. Daughter of the absconding rockstar, whom she never knew. The pendant is her mother's, always had it — not found on Deborah's bedside — and is the terminal's tracker. Half-angel and ineligible for sorting: nepotism, not tragedy. Faith is functional; God is her employer and she has views about management. Treats divine instruction as an unreliable supplier. Finds being called a saint ridiculous.

relations.note: Nina never knew her father; the pendant was the terminal's tracker.

characters.name: PC Kath Bridges
characters.description: White British police officer in her thirties. Sincerely believes she was left behind to teach moral justice; cannot remember who said so. Maintains paperwork and cites vanished superiors. Notices the wrong details with total commitment. Mild grievance, never fear or amazement. Thinks Ray is the one who gets carried away.

relations.note: Each thinks the other gets carried away.

characters.name: PC Ray Okonjo
characters.description: Black British police officer in his thirties. Sincerely believes he was left behind to teach moral justice; cannot remember who said so. Maintains paperwork and cites vanished superiors. Follows the wrong details nowhere. Mild grievance, never fear or amazement. Thinks Kath is the one who gets carried away.

relations.note: Each thinks the other gets carried away.

characters.name: Danny Crane
characters.description: Forty, olive waxed jacket, canvas satchel, untidy dark hair and stubble. Scavenging for water with his daughter Jodie. Has rules: nothing off anyone still alive. Cannot let her be right because the rules are the last bit of parenting he has. Keeps a laminated rules card. Dry and occupied by logistics, never played for grief.

relations.note: Father and daughter scavenging for water; rules versus practical experience.

characters.name: Jodie Crane
characters.description: Eleven, short sandy hair, navy hoodie under an oversized olive jacket, backpack and a headlamp on her collar. The headlamp stays off in Number Fourteen. Better at crime than Danny and knows it without cruelty. Sees his rules will get them killed. Her mother was raptured and judged worthy. No pathos performance.

relations.note: Father and daughter scavenging for water; rules versus practical experience.

characters.name: Martin
characters.description: Failed musician in a denim jacket correct in 1994, hair long at the back on principle. Four guitars, nothing written in eleven years. Collected the rockstar's belongings at estate sales; won the terminal at auction and has it filed as period junk. Cannot reach his son. Aggrieved rather than grieving. Never learns what the machine is.

relations.note: Martin cannot reach his son; Max borrowed the terminal for a poster.

characters.name: Max
characters.description: Fourteen-year-old son of Martin, making a retro poster for his esports team The Raptors. Misspells it RAPTURES, balances moral-criterion bars as graphic design, sets opponents weak. Machine shows ERROR, cut straight to UNDO? (prologue shot 31 cut). Asks to clear past attempts, then minimises the window. Alive, unreachable; flashbacks only. Worried he is in trouble, not wracked with guilt. The series does not laugh at him.

relations.note: Martin cannot reach his son; Max borrowed the terminal for a poster.

characters.name: Brenda
characters.description: Limbo guide in her fifties, cardigan over robes behind a folding table. Thirty years in post; customer-service warmth. Sincere and bored. Cannot tell the religions apart any more. Has no records on anyone. Talks over the cathedral's four-second reverberation.

relations.note: Thirty years behind the desk, no records on anyone.

characters.name: Gordon
characters.description: Limbo guide in his sixties, cardigan over robes behind a folding table. Thirty years in post; customer-service warmth. Sincere and bored. Cannot tell the religions apart any more. Has no records on anyone. Talks over the cathedral's four-second reverberation.

relations.note: Thirty years behind the desk, no records on anyone.

characters.name: Vassago
characters.description: Hell's intake manager in his fifties, short sleeves and a lanyard. In charge, no idea. More concerned with deflating birthday balloons than the intake collapse. Instantly accepts Tamsin's theory that Heaven stole the damned for its numbers. Investigates entirely the wrong thing.

relations.note: Hell's intake floor.
He adopts her stolen-queue theory immediately.

characters.name: Reek
characters.description: Hell intake employee in his thirties. Has no opinions. Works on a grey corporate open-plan floor with a blank target board and deflating birthday balloons. Goes along with the theory that Heaven stole their queue. In the field he does the leaning-in and the demonic voice, then runs out of material and sits on the floor. Still not frightened of anything except wasting time.

relations.note: Hell's intake floor.
Investigating the wrong thing together.

characters.name: Tamsin
characters.description: Keen Hell intake employee in her twenties carrying a folder. Proposes that Heaven stole the damned to improve its numbers. Her idea becomes the working theory immediately. Investigates the wrong thing all season. Starts enjoying being a person. In the field she interviews blanks like a survey, writing down Wales and I can only apologise with equal confidence.

relations.note: He adopts her stolen-queue theory immediately.
Investigating the wrong thing together.

characters.name: Pat
characters.description: A demon disguised as an old lady in her seventies. Too much rouge, too many doilies, a tin containing only boiled sweets and a husband whose name changes. A cupboard of bottled water she never drinks: not bait, just a demon who doesn't drink sitting on the most valuable thing in the county. Keeps a blank chained under the floor with Malcolm; the apology comes up through the locked door. She is waiting for nothing and the burglars pick her house by chance. Keeps an arrangement going after violence but is frosty as after a parking dispute. Distinct from the woman at Number Fourteen; never substitute that woman's sheet for Pat.

relations.note: Keep the blank chained under the floor; they argue about method and neither learns anything.

characters.name: Malcolm
characters.description: Pat's other half in the overcommitted disguise: cardigan, slippers, perfectly ordinary. Comes up out of the cellar under the stairs and turns the key behind him. Washes his hands to the elbow and hangs the tea towel back on its hook, square. Thinks the chained blank will break, cannot accept that there is nothing in him to break, and is quietly furious that it keeps apologising. The blank he and Pat keep under the floor is Graham.

relations.note: Keep the blank chained under the floor; they argue about method and neither learns anything.

characters.name: Hell's third field officer
characters.description: A female demon with a blank chained in a cellar. Interrogating him about the missing damned, gets only the apology. Reads it as resistance by the system rather than a man doing what he is told. Has notes and thinks she is close. Surveillance grammar, never moving or close.

characters.name: Hariel
characters.description: One of the Michael-adjacent recovery pair, in his forties, linen, immaculate. Sent down to recover the absconder's equipment with permissions rather than power. Fronts the pair: dead centre, perfectly composed, entirely unbothered, and has not read the report either. Smug rather than stupid and of no use whatsoever. Named in the episode-three cold open; no further backstory supplied.

relations.note: Recover the missing equipment.

characters.name: Soqed
characters.description: One of the Michael-adjacent recovery pair, in his thirties, linen, immaculate, always slightly behind Hariel. Has not read the report and admits it. Suggests using a blank because everyone's using them; that is what they're for. Smug rather than stupid and equally useless. Named in the episode-three cold open; no further backstory supplied.

relations.note: Recover the missing equipment.

characters.name: Alan
characters.description: A blank in his fifties, fleece and sensible shoes, carrying a bag for life containing another bag. Nina picks him up at a wrong lockup. The apology is not a reliable test. Not automatically the chained man from the basement; no identity link has been supplied.

characters.name: The absconder
characters.description: An angel who steals a terminal to live inside creation in 1980. Edits appearance, charisma, confidence and musical ability to the ceiling, leaves social status at default. Conjures a guitar; writes by entering tempo and key. Pockets the tracker off the machine's casing; in the montage, a flash of him fastening it round a girl's neck as a keepsake. Nina's father. Dies five years later and declines undo with NO. Prologue fix: shot 12 pockets tracker plus flash montage, shot 31 cut straight from ERROR to UNDO?. Appearance and age are not locked.

relations.note: Nina never knew her father; the pendant was the terminal's tracker.

characters.name: The Woman — Number Fourteen
characters.description: Woman in her fifties with grey-brown hair in an untidy bun, rumpled tan housecoat over a floral blouse, and a Tesco bag stuffed with crumpled papers. Mid-sentence when the door opens. Plays her situation as house rules and a complaint to the council. The table set for six is never played. No visible listener. This supporting character is not Pat and is not identified as a blank or demon.

characters.name: The rescued blank
characters.description: A man chained in a cellar by Hell's third field officer. Gives the apology, doing what he is told. Rescued by Danny and Jodie; talks about laminate flooring. Hell watches through him, putting the rescuers on its map. Do not assume this is Alan. No name or age supplied.

characters.name: Graham
characters.description: A blank in his fifties interviewed by Hell's intake in his own front room. Beige cardigan over a shirt and tie, corduroys, slippers. Perfectly content, hands on knees, facing slightly away from anyone. Answers everything helpfully and is never frightened; the drink is hospitality. Most animated on payroll: the wages, but the deductions as well, statutory and voluntary. Says I can only apologise with no pause at all and apologises for never having made a decision. By the episode-four cold open he is the blank chained under Pat's floor, and his apology comes up through the locked door. Not Alan; whether he is also the blank Danny and Jodie rescue in episode five has not been supplied.

notes.title: Start here — scope, timing and image status
notes.content:
8 × 45min British black comedy. Eight episode outlines and a cast bible are supplied; this is NOT eight completed 45-minute scripts. Episode One revised running order: mugging, St Jude's, cops (first beat), washing up (Nina Sc3, pendant is mother's always had it), Martin storage as pre-rapture flashback (machine eight weeks in Max's room), Danny and Jodie first appearance (21 shots, 148s), cops second beat (6 shots, 90s, 90s), then 1980 tag — roughly 42 minutes. Number Fourteen is fully boarded (13 shots, 175-second working estimate). The numbered cold opens: the episode-three angels (15 shots, 125-second estimate), Graham's interview — an episode-three scene since the restructure, circling what a blank is with the cops' test (17 shots, 172-second estimate), fully studied, the episode-four Pat-and-Malcolm dusk open (16 shots, 151-second estimate, Graham already chained under the floor), fully studied, the scout-hut scene 3 (17 shots, 159-second estimate), fully studied, and Scene 2 — the old-lady sequence — is numbered (35 shots, 305-second estimate), two grammars never blended within a shot, fully studied. The first wrong lockup is numbered (31 shots, 271-second estimate), boarded with AI-generated studies pending production review. Each explicit pause remains exactly as written.

Eight legacy reference boards (cold open, St Jude's, storage facility, police/car park, Limbo, first raid, Hell intake, Wave 3 night drive) plus fully boarded washing up (26 shots FIX 4) are attached to their scenes as ordered keyframes, status Needs review — 157 keyframes plus 3 cards holding the slots of missing files (ep2s2-15.jpg, ep2s3-15.jpg, ep2s3-16.jpg). Shot type, movement, lens and the 5s durations on those boards are working placeholders; review every keyframe against the current grammar before production. Nothing outside Number Fourteen is approved coverage. Unpictured roles have deliberate initials placeholders, not missing files.

The full current source is docs/rapture/show-bible.md. The screenplay sources are docs/rapture/scenes/ep4-number-fourteen.md, docs/rapture/scenes/ep4-cold-open.md, docs/rapture/scenes/ep4-pat-cold-open.md, docs/rapture/scenes/ep4-pat-house.md, docs/rapture/scenes/ep4-scout-hut.md and docs/rapture/scenes/ep3-cold-open.md. notes.title: Series bible — the cause
notes.content:
In 1980 an angel absconds. He doesn't want to administer creation, he wants to live inside it — so he steals a terminal, comes down, and edits his own appearance, confidence, charisma and musical ability to the ceiling. He leaves social status at default and never touches it. He conjures a guitar, writes a song by entering tempo and key, and becomes a rock star. He pockets the tracker off the machine's casing. In the montage, a flash of him fastening it round a girl's neck — the girl he loves — as a keepsake. Five years later he dies of a heart attack in a hotel room, and when the machine asks whether he'd like to undo it, he says no.

The terminal passes through an estate into unclaimed storage. Forty-five years later Martin, a failed musician who has spent his life collecting that rockstar's belongings, wins the lot at auction and brings home a beige box he assumes is period junk. His fourteen-year-old son Max asks to borrow something authentically old for an esports team poster. Max misspells his team name — The Raptors — as RAPTURES, types the tagline LET THE RAPTURES COMMENCE, and is presented with a parameter menu he takes for a character-stat card. The fields are moral criteria: mercy, honesty, restraint, charity. He shuffles the values between fields so the bars look balanced on the poster, sets them below average because in a game you want the enemies weak. The machine shows ERROR. Cut straight to UNDO?. He asks the machine to clear his team's past attempts — meaning two seasons of bad placements he doesn't want on the card — then minimises the window, which sends the signal.

Four billion people are sorted by a child's layout decision. The criteria are decoupled from their values, so the sorting is not corrupt, it is arbitrary — and nobody on earth or in the afterlife can find the pattern, because there isn't one. Nobody is logged in above the dead angel to stop any of it.

notes.title: Series bible — tone
notes.content:
Black comedy. Dry, deadpan, English. Douglas Adams and Dirk Gently for the bureaucracy. The police are stupid in the manner of Dirk Gently or Common Side Effects — loose dialogue, wrong details noticed at length, long pauses, no punchlines.

This is not noir and not a tragedy. The visual styles differ by thread; the register never does. Every thread is the same comedy, shot differently. No pathos beats, no quiet melancholy inserts, no reflective endings, no grief. The grim material is texture.

Nobody in the series knows they're in an apocalypse — they know they're in a situation, and each character has translated the end of the world into the terms they already used. The cops got a promotion. Hell has a reporting problem. Grandma was vindicated. Martin's provenance has been ruined.

Let the funny thing be the sad thing and don't choose between them. Let the bureaucracy be sincere — the guides genuinely need the branch of Christianity for the form. Nothing dramatic ever happens dramatically: the rapture, the violence and the correction all occur with no flash, no sound and no score, and the camera keeps operating as though the subject has merely walked out of frame.

notes.title: Series bible — cosmology
notes.content:
No God and no AI god. Separate universes for each religion, and an administration between them. Nobody ever meets God; nobody can get one on the phone. The whole thing has been running on an administrative layer left on autopilot — angels don't have power, they have permissions.

Limbo is a cathedral: stone, vaulting, stained glass a hundred feet up throwing coloured light on everyone, ceiling vanishing into haze. And bolted into it, the admin — rope barriers screwed into marble, a ticket dispenser cable-tied to a pillar, folding tables with laminated signs, a modern LED departures board zip-tied over something ancient. Packed with four billion irritated people of every religion, all absorbed in the queue rather than the fact of being dead, none of them looking up. Four desks open. Now serving: 41. Sorting has stalled, so nothing moves, and the guides have no records on anyone.

Hell is a corporate open-plan floor. Grey carpet tiles, hot desks, one strip light out, a blank target board, somebody's deflating birthday balloons. Intake has collapsed. Everyone there is thick as fuck.

Limbo is unaffected by time.

notes.title: Series bible — the blanks (npcs)
notes.content:
They always existed — accountants, the ones who bore you to death, the men who do everything their wife tells them and apologise if they get it wrong. Baseline. The rapture didn't damage them; a few started glitching afterwards, and Heaven and Hell now use them as cameras, because an unrendered person is an unguarded window.

Their tell is "I can only apologise" — a complete response with nothing behind it. No reason, no excuse, no defensiveness, nothing to argue with. Half of real humanity says it too, which makes every test for them worthless, and the cops will build a screening method out of it and never doubt it. Limbo has no records on them. Nobody can be told apart from a merely tedious man. Nicknames vary by faction: extras, blanks, monos, greycoats.

notes.title: Series bible — season clock: the water
notes.content: Nobody's left who knows how to run a pump, and nobody is dosing the reservoirs. Fine in ep1 (one ignored complaint about pressure), brown by ep3, upstairs taps dead by ep5, dry by ep6, people dying of it dully by ep7. The apocalypse is a maintenance backlog. The only clean water left is sitting in houses, which is what makes the burglaries inevitable and what the cops are enforcing property law over.

notes.title: Series bible — cast
notes.content:
Sister Nina Doyle, 45. Runs St Jude's, a residential house for people the system gave up on. Stubborn, self-sufficient, won't accept help, lies fluently to authority, can re-plumb a building. Says a thing once and acts as though it's settled. Gentle with the genuinely broken, brutal with anyone coasting. Her faith is functional — God is her employer and she has views about the management. Daughter of the 1980 rockstar; never knew him, and assumed her mother's story was a fantasy. The pendant is her mother's, always had it — not found on Deborah's bedside. It is the terminal's tracker. Half-angel, therefore ineligible for sorting, which she'd find annoying rather than tragic — forty-five years of vocation and it turns out to be nepotism. Treats divine instruction as an unreliable supplier sending vague orders, and complains upward. Other people start calling her a saint. She finds this ridiculous and can't get rid of them.

PC Kath Bridges (white, 30s) and PC Ray Okonjo (black, 30s). Sincerely believe they were left behind to teach moral justice and can't remember who told them that. Terrible officers. Never frightened, never amazed; their emotional response to the apocalypse is mild grievance. They maintain paperwork religiously and cite superiors who no longer exist. They notice the wrong things with total commitment and follow them nowhere. Each thinks the other is the one who gets carried away.

Danny, 40, and Jodie, 11. Scavenging for water. He has rules — nothing off anyone still alive — and she can already see the rules are going to get them killed. She's better at crime than he is and knows it, without cruelty. He can't let her be right because the rules are the last bit of parenting he's got. Her mother was raptured.

Martin, 40s. Failed musician. Denim jacket correct in 1994, hair long at the back on principle, four guitars, nothing written in eleven years. Spent his life hunting the rockstar's belongings at estate sales. Owns the machine and has it filed as period junk. Can't reach his son. Aggrieved rather than grieving. Never finds out what the machine is.

Max, 14. Flashbacks only, alive, unreachable. Not wracked with guilt over four billion people — worried he's in trouble. Trash-talks his mates while setting their values. The one character the series doesn't laugh at.

Brenda (50s) and Gordon (60s). Limbo guides. Folding table, cardigans over robes, customer-service warmth, thirty years in post. Sincere. Bored. Cannot tell the religions apart any more.

Vassago (50s, short sleeves, lanyard, in charge, no idea), Reek (30s, no opinions), Tamsin (20s, keen, folder). Hell's intake. They don't notice the collapse for ages because they're worried about the balloons. Tamsin proposes that Heaven has stolen their damned for the numbers; it becomes the working theory instantly, and they investigate entirely the wrong thing all season. Tamsin starts enjoying being a person.

Pat, 70s. A demon running Hell's audit disguised as an old lady, because nobody suspects her and she can ask the most invasive questions on earth and have it read as nosiness. Disguise overcommitted: too many doilies, a tin containing only boiled sweets, too much rouge, a husband whose name changes. A cupboard of bottled water she never drinks — not bait, just a demon who doesn't drink sitting on the most valuable thing in the county. Graham is chained under her floor and his apology comes up through the locked door. She's waiting for nothing, and the burglars pick her house by chance. She'll keep an arrangement going after violence and be a bit frosty about it, like a neighbour after a parking dispute.

Malcolm, 70s. Pat's other half in the disguise: cardigan, slippers, perfectly ordinary. Comes up out of the cellar and turns the key behind him, washes his hands to the elbow, hangs the tea towel back on its hook, square. Thinks Graham will break; cannot accept that there's nothing in him to break; quietly furious that he keeps apologising.

Hell's third field officer. Has a blank chained in a cellar and is interrogating it to find out where the damned went. All she gets is the apology, which she reads as the system refusing to break. It's just a man doing what he's told. She has notes. She thinks she's close.

Two angels. Sent down to recover the absconder's missing equipment. Smug rather than stupid, and equally useless.

Alan, 50s. A blank Nina picks up. Fleece, sensible shoes, a bag for life containing another bag.

notes.title: Series bible — visual grammar — one per thread, never mixed
notes.content:
- Nina — locked off, wide, deep focus, daylight, symmetrical. The camera never follows her; she walks into frames and out of them. Long lenses on the road. The only handheld in her thread is the vision.
- Cops — static two-shot through the windscreen from the bonnet, plus a wide from across the car park. Sitcom frame, boring, symmetrical. Handheld only when they commit violence, then straight back to the identical framing as if nothing happened. No reaction cuts.
- Danny & Jodie — handheld, tight, dark. Red practical sources only: a bike light, a torch with a red filter, a standby LED. Never a wide establishing shot; we never see a whole room.
- Limbo — frontal, proscenium, Python staging. Vertical compositions with people tiny at the base, very low angles looking up into nothing, then hard cuts to the desk, flat and close. Every word at the desk reverberates four seconds; the guides talk over it, nobody else has learned to. Crowded.
- Hell / demons on earth — surveillance. Fixed high-corner cameras, 4:3, faint burnt-in timecode, slight fisheye. Cut between fixed angles only. Never moves, never close.
- Martin — fluorescent, flat, unlovely. Locked off, framings slightly off-centre. Institutional beige.
- 1980 — warm, grainy, anamorphic, heavy practical sources through net curtains. Sodium and tungsten. Deliberately beautiful.
- The visions — total break in style. Wrong aspect ratio, dropped frames, blown out, a hiss. Badly exposed home video, not white light and choral swell. She's receiving the tracker's recorded view, not God's plan.
- Episode eight, the arcade — all grammars collapse. Neutral, ordinary, unstyled. The only location in the series shot in no style at all.

notes.title: Series bible — connective objects
notes.content:
Things travel between threads; characters mostly don't. The knife from the cold open, in the old woman's handbag, into the support group, and eventually to Jodie. The pendant — her mother's, always had it, not found on Deborah's bedside — which is Nina's bearing and everyone else's tracker — every use lights her up for Heaven and Hell, so every clue costs her a head start. In the prologue montage, a flash of the absconder fastening it round a girl's neck. Max's minimised window, whose signal draws all four factions to the same postcode. The boring blank Danny and Jodie rescue, which Hell is watching through — so the kindest act in the series puts the group on Hell's map.

Prologue fixes: shot 12 — pockets the tracker (plus flash in montage of fastening round girl's neck). Shot 31 — cut; go straight from ERROR to UNDO?.

Nobody ever explains the whole thing to anyone. No catch-up scenes. Each character ends the season understanding about 30% of what happened. The audience is the only one holding all of it.

notes.title: Series bible — episodes
notes.content:
1 — no mechanism revealed. The mugging. Nina Sc 1 — St Jude's and the rapture. The cops — birds, arrest ourselves, the taser. Nina Sc 3 — washing up and aftermath, the pendant (her mother's, always had it, not Deborah's bedside), the first vision, she drives. Martin's auction — marked as pre-rapture flashback, since the machine must have been in Max's room for eight weeks. Then Danny and Jodie — first appearance, three weeks in, they do this now and she's better at it (handheld, tight, dark, red practical light, never a clean wide). Then the cops second beat — static two-shot from the bonnet, same bottle untouched, ends comic thread worse than it started (ninety seconds). Tag: 1980, ending on NO. Roughly 42 minutes before tag.

Fixes: Prologue 12 pockets tracker (65mm static small dull red pulse) + flash 24f montage fastening round girl neck (16mm handheld over-exposed hotel corridor dressing room half second); Prologue 31 cut ERROR→UNDO? (30 STATUS ACTIVE ERROR → 32 SLOW PUSH UNDO?); Ep1 Sc3 FIX 4 fully boarded 26 shots — shot 18 cut (pendant among dead woman's things Deborah), shots 23-24 replaced — 23 STATIC MEDIUM 50mm her own room single bed cross crooked bedside drawer elastic bands rosary broken link nail file pendant dull, 24 CLOSE 65mm picks up because in way of torch batteries forty years never worn puts on practical smaller round neck bag vision beat same corridor hand to chest; Ep4 cold open move to dusk (16:12:04 to 19:51:32) continuous into Scene 2 old lady 35 shots; Martin's auction marked pre-rapture flashback (machine 8 weeks in Max room flat fluorescent); Ep3 meeting trimmed to recruitment only (grandma dog + nun moved to Ep5 therapy); Ep5 therapy class 26 shots brown rationed water final + Night at Pat's 51 shots replaces previous Pat's house version No CCTV two grammars only cops static 32mm windscreen handheld only for violence Danny Jodie handheld close dark red torchlight demons only in torch beam.

2 — there's an afterlife and it's badly run. Limbo: the family, the branches of Christianity, the seventy-two virgins, the husband led away. Danny and Jodie's first raid. Hell's intake floor. Nina's first wrong lockup; she acquires Alan.

3 — blanks, and both sides come down. Demons and angels arrive, badly. The blanks established. The cops invent a worthless test. Danny and Jodie recruited by the underground group. Brown water. Martin comes home to a collection and no son.

4 — the old lady. Jodie on the settee, Danny in the kitchen, the knife and fork, the fork through the forearm, the bottles by the gate. Scout hut recruitment trimmed to recruitment only — twelve litres, rota, 'tins don't count', Jodie working out who's stealing. Grandma/dog and nun moved to Episode Five therapy class.

5 — therapy + the night at Pat's. Therapy class revised — 26 shots, INT. THE SCOUT HUT DAY, handheld close faces circle not quite circle red fire door light tarpaulin never wide. Hi-vis clipboard facilitator, Sue 50s blameless furious, Carl 30s knows what he did, Derek 60s sober 22 years insufferable, Pauline 40s wants to write to someone, Danny/Jodie at edge not participating. Safe space/scout hut, laminated sheet writing down who doesn't, never done anything/cat note, forty years careful Linda horrible, everybody's problem, clerical mistake/Because, who do you write to/look into it, Carl quiet too quickly nothing they'd take you for, modesty/Jodie does not, Rosemary next door dog rug Thursday went up straight up, that bad, long hold silence dead dog demolishes room (protection), what we're for invented on spot (protection), kept us back work/keep order doctrine, promoted maintain order, divine mandate in ninety seconds no objections, Derek moment of clarity 2003, end of world not same as divorce very similar, one day at a time most useful thing in eight weeks, not pleased, empty chair Brian went out Tuesday, nobody follows up, Jodie at edge adults guessing, Danny sleeve over bandage, final wide brown and rationed water not two days left. Protections: Carl never says what he did. Doctrine needs time to harden before 7-8. Then the night at Pat's — 51 shots, EXT./INT. PAT'S ROAD AND HOUSE NIGHT, replaces previous Pat's house version. No CCTV anywhere. Two grammars only: cops static two-shot through windscreen 32mm locked off handheld only for violence, Danny and Jodie handheld close dark red torchlight, demons only ever seen in someone's torch beam. Kath Ray Danny Jodie Pat Malcolm Neil (50s blank talks about flooring). Stakeout crisps bottle untouched, six bottles at gate, Jodie door under stairs nobody doesn't look, rules taking him off himself, Pat facing fireplace, DO NOT FEED, Neil chained bike lock 1234 old people laminate membrane, slippers tea mouth too wide tea still held, chaotic tea everywhere Neil walks past, head turned all way round, first handheld for cops Police Stop there please, taser form, cuffs their faces go, secure premises, side by side Pat Malcolm knife fork fish slice black eyes smiling Out, sprint everyone in seatbelt, doesn't start it starts, Bring my bottles back love same framing as shot 2, five people in car grammar restored That was drugs condition, arrested forever till something opens, Say sorry I can only apologise first one delighted, evidence cup holder, I'd have to check, laminate, tiny headlights 135mm CUT. Max misspelling flashback remains.

6 — dry. The taps fail completely, upstairs dead system-wide, doctrine from therapy class hardening into religion. Group starts acting on 'maintain order' in 7-8. One day at a time remains only useful advice. Nina gets a bearing that isn't wrong and is found by people who've decided she's a saint (nun rumour from therapy points at her). The cops arrest a demon and paperwork won't stick. Max flashback: stat bars.

7 — convergence. Four parties, four wrong reasons, one postcode. Martin already there with the machine plugged in, trying to make it play something. Limbo: someone in administration realises nobody is auditing them either. Max flashback: "just clear our past attempts."

8 — the arcade. Everyone in one building, all wrong about why. Martin defends his collection from people trying to save the world. The cops arrest people in sequence. Demons and angels arrive simultaneously and each assumes the other is what they came for. Upstairs: Jodie gets through because she's eleven and ignored; Nina can't read the menu; Max knows where the fields are. The reversal won't authorise — Limbo administration is protecting the outage, because a stalled queue means nobody audits them. Nina wins an argument at a desk. Then the correction: not a rewind, but a bid on an auction lot, placed by a nun, outbidding Martin for the box the machine is in. ENTER. No flash, no sound.

Last shots. The storage unit, shutter down, the machine unopened in the dark. The lot sticker: a number, a date, SOLD. Then Limbo, untouched by time, the queue exactly as it was, and a man at the desk saying he's just got one question. No epilogue, no faces, nothing resolved for anyone.

notes.title: Series bible — output format
notes.content: Numbered shots. Each shot: shot type, lens, how the camera is mounted, then a short plain description. Dialogue indented beneath the shot it falls in. Mark pauses in seconds where the pause is the joke. No scene-setting prose, no camera poetry, no explanation of subtext.

notes.title: Continuity decisions and open questions
notes.content:
The latest series prompt takes precedence over the earlier visual canon. Danny and Jodie now have no wide establishing shots, no complete-room views and no sodium/teal look. In Number Fourteen, shot 1 is a CU/50mm of the headlight switch and shot 12 a MS/35mm of the passing van panel. All dialogue, numbered beats and pauses are unchanged. White headlights are not shown. The old version remains archived.

Number Fourteen's woman is the sheet-27 house-rules character, not Pat. The new episode-four Pat sequence remains a separate outline and has not been silently replaced by this scene. No blanks or afterlife appear in Number Fourteen. No cosmology is added to its dialogue.

The woman describes a locally intermittent upstairs tap in episode four; the series-wide upstairs failure remains episode five.

Max remains flashbacks only, alive and unreachable. Episode eight says he knows where the fields are; how that knowledge reaches the upstairs action is not specified, so no present-day reunion has been invented.

The cause retains 1980, death five years later and forty-five years later exactly as supplied. A present-day calendar year has not been silently inferred. Nina remains 45.

The chained/rescued blank is not silently identified as Alan. The third field officer and the recovery angels remain unnamed. The 1980 absconder's appearance is not locked. Confirm exact van plates and jacket-pocket continuity before approving images.

In the episode-four cold open Graham is the blank chained under Pat's floor: the apology he gave Hell's intake with no pause at all now arrives from behind the locked cellar door at dusk, muffled and entirely calm, heard and never seen. He remains not Alan and has no surname; whether the episode-three interview's front room is Pat's front room, and whether the blank Danny and Jodie rescue in episode five is also Graham, has not been supplied and no link is asserted. His glitch — repeating the shot-10 clause to an empty room in shot 15 — is played completely flat with no sting, no cut and no camera move; the timecode burn-in carries the five-hour jump. Reek and Tamsin keep their intake-floor surveillance grammar in the field: 4:3 high-corner framing, slight fisheye and a visible advancing timecode.

The episode-three cold open names the recovery angels Hariel and Soqed; no further backstory is supplied. Their grammar is the opposite of Hell's: immaculate, centred, advert-like, no timecode. The unnamed MAN (60s, cardigan) between the pallets of bark chippings is a blank who belongs to nobody and joins no cast list. The two cold opens never share a frame with another faction; the episode-eight collapse to neutral coverage has not happened yet.

3 legacy keyframes are missing from disk and hold placeholder slots: ep2s2-15.jpg, ep2s3-15.jpg, ep2s3-16.jpg.

brainstorm.title: The knife
brainstorm.content: Cold open → old woman's handbag → support group → Jodie. A connective object, not a catch-up conversation.

brainstorm.title: The pendant / tracker
brainstorm.content: Nina's bearing, everyone else's tracker. Each use costs a head start. Visions are recordings, not God's plan.

brainstorm.title: The minimised window
brainstorm.content: RAPTURES → balanced stat bars → clear past attempts → minimise. The signal draws four factions to one postcode.

brainstorm.title: The water clock
brainstorm.content: Ep1 pressure complaint ignored; ep3 brown; ep5 upstairs dead; ep6 dry; ep7 dull deaths. Clean water in houses drives crime and property enforcement.

brainstorm.title: The rescued blank
brainstorm.content: The kindest act puts the group on Hell's map. A boring man discussing laminate flooring is an unguarded window.

script:
LET THE RAPTURES COMMENCE
EPISODE ONE — DANNY AND JODIE

INT./EXT. A HOUSE — DUSK
Cast: DANNY (40), JODIE (11)
Grammar: handheld, tight, dark, red practical light. Never a clean wide.

This is three weeks in and it's their first appearance. It should establish only two things: they do this now, and she's better at it.


1. EXT. BACK GARDEN — HANDHELD, 35mm, dusk
A fence. Danny goes over it badly, catching his coat. Jodie goes over it in one movement and waits.

2. HANDHELD — 28mm, close, the back door
He's got a screwdriver in the frame. It isn't going well. She watches.
   JODIE: It's not that sort of lock.
   DANNY: It is.
   JODIE: It's the other sort.

3. INSERT — 85mm, handheld
The screwdriver slips. His knuckle goes into the frame.

4. HANDHELD — 28mm
Jodie leans past him, does something to the handle, and the door opens.

5. HANDHELD CLOSE — 50mm
Danny holding a screwdriver, looking at an open door.
   DANNY: It was already —
   JODIE: Mm.

6. INT. KITCHEN — HANDHELD, 28mm, red torchlight
Inside. Close and shifting. A cupboard door, a corner of worktop, half a calendar. Never the room.
   DANNY: (low) Rules.
   JODIE: (recited, bored) Nothing off anyone still alive. Nothing off the dead that's got a name on it. No upstairs.
   DANNY: And?
   JODIE: And check the cistern.

7. INSERT — 100mm macro, handheld
Cupboards opening. Tins. A great deal of chutney. Nothing useful.

8. HANDHELD — 35mm
Danny finds a four-pint bottle of water at the back of a cupboard. Half full. He's thrilled and trying not to show it.

9. HANDHELD CLOSE — 50mm, on JODIE
She's looking at the ceiling.
   JODIE: There's a coat on the bannister.
   DANNY: So?
   JODIE: It's a going-out coat.

10. HANDHELD — 28mm
He stops. Listens. The house is completely still.
   DANNY: They're gone.
   JODIE: You don't know that.
   DANNY: Everyone's gone.
   JODIE: Not everyone.

11. HANDHELD — 35mm, hallway, very dark
Jodie goes toward the downstairs loo. Her bike light swings across a wall of framed photographs. Twenty of them, the same two people.

12. HANDHELD CLOSE — 50mm
She stops. Not moved. Assessing.
   JODIE: (calling, not loud) Dad.
   DANNY: (o.s.) What.
   JODIE: How many people d'you reckon are still here?
   DANNY: (o.s.) Don't know.
   JODIE: One in ten? One in twenty?
   DANNY: (o.s.) Do the cistern, Jodie.

13. INSERT — 85mm, handheld
The cistern lid off. She dips a bottle and fills it, entirely unbothered.

14. HANDHELD — 28mm, kitchen
A sound upstairs. One dull thump.

15. HANDHELD CLOSE — 50mm, on DANNY
Rigid. Not brave.

16. HANDHELD — 28mm, foot of the stairs
The two of them, close, whispering.
   DANNY: Out. Now.
   JODIE: It'll be a cat.
   DANNY: Out.
   JODIE: It's always a cat.
   DANNY: (hissing) One time it wasn't a cat.

17. HANDHELD — 35mm, up the stairwell, red, nothing visible
Hold. Then another thump, and something falling over.

18. HANDHELD — chaotic, 28mm
They go, fast and badly, knocking into things. He drops the screwdriver. She doesn't drop the water.

19. EXT. ALLEY — HANDHELD, 35mm
Both against a wall, breathing hard. Bags between their feet.
   JODIE: It was a cat.
   DANNY: You don't know that.
   JODIE: (holding up the cistern bottle) We could've had the upstairs one. Header tank's better.
   DANNY: (a beat) What's a header tank?
   JODIE: (genuinely pleased) Exactly.

20. HANDHELD CLOSE — 50mm, on DANNY
A man who has just been overtaken by his eleven-year-old and is deciding whether to acknowledge it.
   DANNY: Don't tell anyone about the door.

21. HANDHELD WIDE — 28mm, alley
The two of them walking away, red bike light bobbing, bags in hand. A completely dark street.
Hold.

LET THE RAPTURES COMMENCE
EPISODE ONE — THE COPS, SECOND BEAT

INT. POLICE CAR — NIGHT (PARKED)
Cast: KATH (30s), RAY (30s)
Grammar: static two-shot from the bonnet. The same bottle of water in the cup holder, untouched.

Short — ninety seconds. Its only job is to end the episode's comic thread on a worse note than it started.


1. STATIC TWO-SHOT — 32mm, locked off, through the windscreen
Dark. Both of them lit by the dashboard. Kath eating. Ray not.

Hold. Four seconds.
   KATH: He'll be all right, that lad.
   RAY: Which lad?
   KATH: The one from the car park.
   RAY: He was thirty-odd.
   KATH: He looked younger.
   RAY: They do.

(Pause. Six seconds.)
   KATH: I only tasered him.
   RAY: I know.
   KATH: People get tasered.
   RAY: They do.

2. STATIC WIDE — 24mm, exterior, from across the road
The car, alone, parked across two bays in an empty street. Interior light on.

3. STATIC TWO-SHOT — as 1
   RAY: There's a form.
   KATH: Ray.
   RAY: I'm only saying there's a form.
   KATH: (a beat) Have you got the form?
   RAY: (immediately) No.

(Pause.)
   KATH: Then there isn't a form.

4. INSERT — 85mm, static
The bottle in the cup holder. Neither of them has drunk any of it.

5. STATIC TWO-SHOT — as 1
Hold. Five seconds.
   RAY: Kath.
   KATH: Mm.
   RAY: Who do you think's in charge now?
   KATH: (no hesitation whatsoever) Us.

6. STATIC WIDE — 24mm, exterior — same framing as shot 2
The car in an empty street, interior light on, two people sat in it.
Hold. CUT.

LET THE RAPTURES COMMENCE
EPISODE 2 — "THE FIRST WRONG LOCKUP"

EXT./INT. ROADS AND AN INDUSTRIAL ESTATE — DAY
Cast: NINA (45), ALAN (50s)
Grammar: locked off, wide, deep focus, daylight, symmetrical. The camera never follows her. Long lenses for the road. Only the vision is handheld: broken, wrong aspect ratio, dropped frames, blown out, a hiss.


1. STATIC WIDE, 135mm, locked off — EXT. DUAL CARRIAGEWAY. Long lens, heat shimmer. The minibus, tiny, on an empty three-lane road. It takes a long time to reach the middle of frame.

2. STATIC MEDIUM, 40mm, locked off — INT. BUS. From the passenger side. Nina driving. The dog on the seat beside her, upright, facing forward like a passenger.
   NINA: Don't look at me.

3. STATIC WIDE, 50mm, locked off — EXT. ROAD. Roadside. She passes a church. A queue outside it, forty people deep. A trestle table. Someone with a clipboard organising badly. Two men arguing at the front.
   The bus goes by without slowing.

4. STATIC WIDE, 35mm, locked off — EXT. ROAD. A roadblock made of three wheelie bins and a garden bench. A teenage boy in a hi-vis vest stands beside it with a cricket bat, entirely alone, guarding a road that goes nowhere.
   The bus drives around it across the grass verge.

5. STATIC MEDIUM, 40mm, locked off — INT. BUS. Nina, unbothered. The dog watches the boy go past.

6. STATIC WIDE, 135mm, locked off — EXT. ROAD. Hand-painted sheets tied to a footbridge. WE ARE THE CHOSEN ONES. Below it, on a second sheet: ROOMS AVAILABLE.

7. STATIC MEDIUM, 40mm, locked off — INT. BUS. She pulls over. Kills the engine. Takes the pendant out of her collar and holds it in her fist like it owes her money.

8. CLOSE, 65mm, static — Her face. Braced. Not reverent. The expression of someone about to get a phone call they've been dreading.

9. FLASH, 25mm, handheld — An orange roller shutter.

10. FLASH, 50mm, handheld — Strip lights in a corridor. One flickering.

11. FLASH, 50mm, handheld — A painted bay number. Two digits. Held a beat too briefly to be certain of the second one.

12. FLASH, 24mm, handheld — Low, six inches off the floor. A carpet. A radiator. Wrong decade.

13. CLOSE, 65mm, static — Nina. Eyes open. Breathing hard. She looks profoundly unimpressed.
    NINA: (to the windscreen) Forty-one, or forty-seven?

14. STATIC MEDIUM, 40mm, locked off — Nothing happens. The dog looks at her.
    NINA: Forty-one or forty-seven?
    (Pause.)
    NINA: (starting the engine) Right.

15. STATIC WIDE, 28mm, locked off — EXT. INDUSTRIAL ESTATE. A low unit behind chain link. Not the one Martin visited. Similar enough. Barrier arm down. Weeds.

16. STATIC WIDE, 24mm, locked off — She gets out. Looks at the barrier. Gets a pair of bolt cutters out of the bus and deals with the chain on the gate in about nine seconds.

17. STATIC WIDE, 24mm, locked off — INT. CORRIDOR. Deep perspective. A corridor of orange roller doors receding to a vanishing point. Strip lights. One flickering.
    She walks away from camera down the middle of it.
    (Same composition as Martin's corridor. Wrong building.)

18. MEDIUM, 50mm, static — She stops at 41. Looks at it. Cuts the padlock. Three attempts — she's stronger than Martin but it's still a padlock.

19. STATIC WIDE, 28mm, locked off — Low. The shutter goes up on a unit containing approximately four hundred plastic garden chairs.

20. MEDIUM, 50mm, static — Nina looks at four hundred garden chairs.

21. STATIC WIDE, 24mm, locked off — Corridor. She walks to 47. Cuts that padlock too.

22. STATIC WIDE, 28mm, locked off — Low. Shutter up. Empty. Completely empty. A concrete floor and a dead wasp.

23. CLOSE, 65mm, static — Nina in the doorway of an empty unit.
    NINA: (upward, conversational) Was it one of the other forty, then?

24. STATIC WIDE, 24mm, locked off — Corridor. Same framing as 17. Her, small, at the far end, in front of a corridor of identical shutters that goes on for a very long way.
    Hold.

25. STATIC WIDE, 28mm, locked off — EXT. ESTATE. She comes out. Loads the bolt cutters. Stops.

26. STATIC MEDIUM, 50mm, locked off — A MAN (50s, fleece, sensible shoes, holding a carrier bag) is standing beside the minibus. Perfectly still. He has been there some time. The dog is looking at him through the window.
    MAN: Is this yours?
    NINA: It is.
    MAN: I thought it might be.
    (Pause. He doesn't move or explain himself.)
    NINA: Can I help you?
    MAN: I've been here since Tuesday.
    NINA: Doing what?
    MAN: (a genuine pause, thinking hard) Waiting.
    NINA: For what?
    MAN: (cheerfully) Well. Nothing's come.

27. CLOSE, 65mm, static — On NINA. She looks at him. Twenty years of assessing people at a front door.
    NINA: What's in the bag?
    MAN: Bag for life.
    NINA: What's *in* it?
    MAN: (looking) Oh. Another bag.

28. STATIC WIDE, 28mm, locked off — Nina considers leaving him there. Properly considers it.
    Then she opens the passenger door.

29. STATIC MEDIUM, 40mm, locked off — Interior. He gets in. Sits perfectly upright. Puts the bag on his knees. Faces forward, exactly like the dog.
    NINA: Name?
    MAN: Alan.
    NINA: Right.
    ALAN: Am I in the way?
    NINA: No.
    ALAN: (immediately, warmly) I can only apologise.

30. CLOSE, 65mm, static — On NINA. She looks at him. Nothing registers. She has no idea what that means.
    She starts the engine.

31. STATIC WIDE, 135mm, locked off — EXT. ROAD. Long lens, heat shimmer. The bus, tiny, pulling away down a long straight road.
    Hold.

LET THE RAPTURES COMMENCE
EPISODE 3 — COLD OPEN

EXT./INT. A PARK AND A GARDEN CENTRE — DAY
Cast: HARIEL (40s, linen, immaculate), SOQED (30s, likewise, slightly behind him always)
Grammar: the opposite of Hell's. Not surveillance — immaculate. Locked off, perfectly composed, centred, slightly too symmetrical. Wide lenses, everything in focus, beautiful light. It looks like an advert. That's the joke: they've made themselves look tremendous and they are of no use whatsoever.


1. EXT. PARK — STATIC WIDE — 28mm, locked off, dead centre, golden light
An empty municipal park. A bandstand. Beautiful.
Two men are standing in the middle of the grass, perfectly composed, facing the same direction. They have been there for some time.
   HARIEL: Right.
   SOQED: Right.

   (Pause. Eight seconds.)

   HARIEL: Where would you keep a computer?

2. STATIC WIDE — 24mm, locked off, symmetrical
The two of them, centred, the bandstand exactly behind them.
   SOQED: I don't know what one looks like.
   HARIEL: You've seen one.
   SOQED: Have I?
   HARIEL: In the report.
   SOQED: I didn't read the report.

   (Pause.)

   HARIEL: (entirely unbothered) No. Nor did I.

3. STATIC MEDIUM — 50mm, locked off, frontal, two-shot
Both facing camera. Nothing behind the eyes, but well-lit.
   HARIEL: It's beige.
   SOQED: Beige.
   HARIEL: That's the main thing about it.

4. EXT. HIGH STREET — STATIC WIDE — 28mm, locked off, centred, lovely light
An empty high street. The two of them walking down the middle of it in perfect step. Broken glass, an overturned bin, a dog in a doorway. Neither of them looks at any of it.

5. STATIC WIDE — 24mm, locked off
They stop outside a shop. Look in the window.

6. INSERT — 85mm, static
A window display of beige garden furniture.

7. STATIC MEDIUM — 50mm, frontal
   SOQED: (quietly, to himself) Beige.
   HARIEL: Not that sort of beige.

8. INT. GARDEN CENTRE — STATIC WIDE — 24mm, locked off, deep perspective, aisles
Enormous, empty, strip-lit. Racks of compost. The two of them walk down the centre aisle, still in step.

9. STATIC WIDE — 28mm, locked off
They stop. In the middle distance, standing between two pallets of bark chippings, facing nothing: a MAN (60s, cardigan, still).

10. STATIC MEDIUM — 50mm, frontal, on the two angels
   HARIEL: There's one.
   SOQED: Is he ours or theirs?
   HARIEL: He's nobody's.
   SOQED: (a beat) Can we use him?
   HARIEL: Everyone's using them. That's what they're for.

11. STATIC WIDE — 28mm, locked off
The blank continues facing nothing. Neither angel approaches him.

12. INSERT — 85mm, static
The blank's eyes. Nothing wrong with them. Nothing behind them either.

13. STATIC TWO-SHOT — 50mm, frontal
   SOQED: So what's the plan?
   HARIEL: We locate the equipment, we recover the equipment, we go home.
   SOQED: And if someone's using it?
   HARIEL: Nobody's using it. They haven't got the permissions.
   SOQED: How do you know?
   HARIEL: (with total confidence) Because they haven't.

14. STATIC WIDE — 24mm, locked off, deep perspective, aisles
The two of them walking away down the centre aisle, in step, immaculate, past the motionless man, in entirely the wrong direction.

Hold.

15. BLACK. TITLE CARD.

LET THE RAPTURES COMMENCE
EPISODE 4 — "NUMBER FOURTEEN"

EXT./INT. NUMBER FOURTEEN — NIGHT
Cast: DANNY (40), JODIE (11), THE WOMAN (number 14, 50s)
Grammar: handheld, tight, dark, red practical sources only.


1. CU, 50mm, handheld — Danny's hand on the headlight switch. The red letterbox light on the wet side window. A 2-second pause. He turns the switch off.

2. MS, 35mm, handheld — the cab. Danny, a laminated card in his hand.
   DANNY: Number 14. The taps run there.
   JODIE: The letterbox is on.
   DANNY: So is the dashboard.
   A 2-second pause.
   DANNY: Rule two. No lights on the street.

3. MS, 35mm, handheld — Danny on the step, red light off the letterbox on his face. He knocks three times.
   A 3-second pause.
   DANNY: (to the door) It's cold.
   A 2-second pause.
   DANNY: (to Jodie, over his shoulder) It's very cold.

4. MS, 35mm, handheld — the door opens. THE WOMAN (50s, rumpled housecoat over a floral blouse, a Tesco bag stuffed with crumpled papers) holding the door for someone.
   THE WOMAN: Oh, sorry, I'm mid-sentence.
   She steps back into the hall, lets the door swing, and reopens it.

5. MS, 35mm, handheld — the hall, over her shoulder. A table set for six, plates on it.
   THE WOMAN: Number 14.
   DANNY: That's what the card says.
   THE WOMAN: I know what the card says.

6. MS, 35mm, handheld — the kitchen, red light only: the letterbox light under the door, the red light of the kettle on. Six cups on the counter.
   THE WOMAN: You want water.
   DANNY: We're looking for water.
   THE WOMAN: The tap. (points) Not the upstairs.
   DANNY: Why not?
   THE WOMAN: Dead most days.
   A 2-second pause.
   THE WOMAN: Was fine on Tuesday. That was Thursday.

7. CU, 50mm, handheld — the tap. The water comes out brown. A 4-second pause of brown water. The water comes out clear.
   JODIE: (quietly) It's doing it again.
   DANNY: Rule nine. Write it down.
   JODIE: I am.

8. MS, 35mm, handheld — Jodie filling the bottle at the sink. The woman watching.
   THE WOMAN: Biscuit.
   A 2-second pause.
   DANNY: We haven't broken any rules.
   THE WOMAN: Rule one is biscuit.

9. CU, 50mm, handheld — Danny. A slow blink. He looks at his card.
   DANNY: I don't have a biscuit.
   A 2-second pause.
   JODIE: I have a biscuit.
   Jodie produces a biscuit from Danny's jacket.
   DANNY: That's from the tin.
   JODIE: The tin's in the van. That's from my pocket.
   Danny looks at the jacket. There is no pocket.
   A 2-second pause.
   Danny writes something on the card.

10. MS, 35mm, handheld — the sink. Jodie offers the biscuit. The woman takes it, eats it, and hands the bottle back. It's full and cold and has the air out of it.
    THE WOMAN: Don't come back on a Tuesday.
    DANNY: Why not?
    THE WOMAN: The pipes.
    A 2-second pause.
    JODIE: That's not a reason.
    A 2-second pause.
    THE WOMAN: It's a reason.

11. MS, 35mm, handheld — the cab. Danny driving. Jodie holding the bottle.
    JODIE: What was she saying?
    DANNY: I think it was about the council.
    JODIE: To who?
    A 2-second pause.
    DANNY: I don't know.

12. MS, 35mm, handheld — the wet side panel of the van passing the door, no lights. The red letterbox light stays on.
    A 2-second pause.

13. MS, 35mm, handheld — number 14's front door, from the street. The door opens. THE WOMAN, mid-sentence.
    THE WOMAN: — and that's why I'm telling the council, the parking, the noise, the —
    A 2-second pause.
    The door closes.
    CUT TO BLACK.

LET THE RAPTURES COMMENCE
EPISODE 4 — COLD OPEN

INT. SUBURBAN FRONT ROOM — DAY
Cast: REEK (30s), TAMSIN (20s), GRAHAM (50s, a blank)
Grammar: fixed high-corner surveillance cameras, 4:3, faint burnt-in timecode, slight fisheye. Cut between fixed angles only. Never moves, never close. The timecode runs on across the cuts, so the audience can see how long this has been going.

Protections: the timecode does the heavy lifting — five hours pass and the joke is entirely in the numbers. "Wales" needs no reaction from anyone but Tamsin writing it down. Shot 15 is the first glitch the audience sees, played completely flat: no music sting, no camera move, just a man repeating a clause about payroll to an empty room.


1. FIXED CAM — high corner, 4:3, timecode 11:04:22
A front room. Graham in the armchair, hands on his knees, facing slightly away from anyone. Reek and Tamsin on the settee, sitting too upright, like people who have been told how chairs work.
   REEK: So. Where did they go.
   GRAHAM: Who's that?
   REEK: The bad ones.
   GRAHAM: (after a genuine pause) Bad ones.
   REEK: The wicked. The unrighteous.
   GRAHAM: (brightening) Oh, I don't know any of them.

2. FIXED CAM — opposite high corner, timecode 11:19:51
Same positions. Tamsin has her folder open on her knee.
   TAMSIN: Have you ever done anything wrong?
   GRAHAM: I took a pen from the office.
   TAMSIN: (writing it down) Right.
   GRAHAM: It was a rollerball.
   TAMSIN: When was this?
   GRAHAM: Ninety-eight.

3. FIXED CAM — high corner, timecode 11:41:07
Reek has got up and is standing over him. Tamsin is still writing.
   REEK: I want you to look at me.
   GRAHAM: Righto.
   REEK: (leaning in, doing something demonic and enormous with his face and voice) LOOK AT ME.
   GRAHAM: (looking at him) Yes.

   (Pause. Six seconds.)

   GRAHAM: Would you like a drink?

4. FIXED CAM — a different angle, the doorway, timecode 11:52:30
Graham has gone to make drinks. Reek and Tamsin stand in the middle of the room.
   TAMSIN: He's not frightened.
   REEK: They're all frightened. That's the whole thing about them.
   TAMSIN: He's offered us a drink.
   REEK: (a beat) He might be being clever.

5. FIXED CAM — high corner, timecode 12:08:14
All three seated again. Three mugs. Nobody has touched theirs.
   TAMSIN: Are you dead?
   GRAHAM: I don't think so.
   TAMSIN: Are you sure?
   GRAHAM: (considering it properly, for a long time) I'd have heard.

6. FIXED CAM — opposite corner, timecode 13:26:48
The light in the room has changed. Nobody has moved.
   REEK: Right. Once more. Four billion people went. Upstairs got the good ones. Where did ours go?
   GRAHAM: Ours?

EPISODE 4 — COLD OPEN

INT. PAT'S HOUSE — DUSK
Cast: PAT (70s), MALCOLM (70s, cardigan, slippers, perfectly ordinary), GRAHAM (o.s., chained behind the cellar door)
Grammar: surveillance grammar, because she's a demon: fixed high-corner cameras, 4:3, faint burnt-in timecode, slight fisheye. Cut between fixed angles only. Never moves, never close.

The point: the cellar is planted before anyone knocks, so Scene 2 plays with the audience knowing there's a man under the floor. The man under the floor is Graham, and the phrase is his: the apology he gave Hell's intake with no pause at all now arrives from behind a locked door, which is its worst use so far. Pat and Malcolm's argument about method is the entire demon plot in eight lines — she's right, he can't accept it, neither will learn anything. The water cupboard is no longer bait; it's just a demon who doesn't drink, sitting on the most valuable thing in the county for no reason. She's waiting for nothing, and the burglars pick her house by chance. The whole open happens while the light goes: dusk at the first timecode, dark by the last.

Then Scene 2 is the old lady sequence as written — Jodie on the settee with the squash and the sweet tin, Danny in the kitchen, the knife and fork, the fork through the forearm, the bottles by the gate — except they picked her house by chance, and the audience already knows what is under the floor.
